definitions.plain_definition: The idea that one thing exists before and is more basic than another thing. Here, it means math exists before and is more fundamental than physical matter.
definitions.used_in_context: Mathematical structure is ontologically prior to physical reality.

definitions.plain_definition: The belief that general ideas like numbers or shapes are just names we make up, not real things that exist on their own.
definitions.used_in_context: The nominalist claims mathematical objects do not exist.

definitions.plain_definition: The belief that abstract ideas like numbers and shapes are real and exist in a non-physical world, separate from our minds.
definitions.used_in_context: The Platonist says math exists in an abstract realm — outside space and time, neither physical nor mental.

definitions.plain_definition: The belief that mathematical statements are not really true, but we pretend they are because it is useful.
definitions.used_in_context: The fictionalist claims mathematical statements are literally false — there are no numbers, no sets, no functions — but useful as tools.

definitions.plain_definition: The ability to cause something to happen or to affect something physically.
definitions.used_in_context: If mathematical objects have no causal power, how do they enforce compliance?

definitions.plain_definition: Unable to cause any change or effect. Something that does not push, pull, or influence anything.
definitions.used_in_context: Abstract objects, by definition, cannot push, pull, or constrain anything. They are causally inert.

definitions.plain_definition: A situation where two things are so different in their basic nature that they cannot be considered the same type of thing.
definitions.used_in_context: Every property of mathematical truth is the opposite of every property of human invention. This is not a marginal discrepancy. It is a categorical mismatch.

definitions.plain_definition: Something that could be different or might not exist at all. It depends on other things.
definitions.used_in_context: Contingent — depends on inventor

definitions.plain_definition: Something that must be true and cannot be false. It exists in all possible worlds.
definitions.used_in_context: Necessary — true in all possible worlds

definitions.plain_definition: Never changing. Stays the same forever.
definitions.used_in_context: Immutable — never changes

definitions.plain_definition: Able to change or be changed.
definitions.used_in_context: Mutable — revised, updated, discarded

definitions.plain_definition: The underlying material or substance that something is made of or depends on.
definitions.used_in_context: Immaterial — not physical

definitions.plain_definition: Never wrong. Cannot make mistakes.
definitions.used_in_context: Infallible — cannot produce false results from true premises

definitions.plain_definition: Able to make mistakes or be wrong.
definitions.used_in_context: Fallible — errors are routine

definitions.plain_definition: The principle that the simplest explanation that fits the facts is usually the best one. Also called Occam's Razor.
definitions.used_in_context: Calling them the same is not parsimony. It is confusion.

definitions.plain_definition: The process of writing down a set of basic rules (axioms) from which all other truths in a system can be logically proven.
definitions.used_in_context: Formal axiomatization appeared approximately 150 years ago

definitions.plain_definition: A specific example or concrete version of a general idea or pattern.
definitions.used_in_context: if physical reality is an instantiation of mathematical structure rather than the other way around

definitions.plain_definition: When different lines of evidence or reasoning from separate fields all point to the same conclusion without anyone trying to make them agree.
definitions.used_in_context: This is not engineered consensus. This is unforced convergence — the kind that matters.

definitions.plain_definition: The principle that evidence from different, independent sources can converge to a single, strong conclusion.
definitions.used_in_context: This is unforced convergence — the kind that matters.

definitions.plain_definition: Specific conditions that, if met, would prove a theory or claim is wrong.
definitions.used_in_context: This paper can be falsified by any of the following:

definitions.plain_definition: Able to be proven false by evidence or experiment. A key feature of scientific theories.

definitions.plain_definition: The ability to produce an effect or cause something to happen.
definitions.used_in_context: Explain the causal efficacy of abstract objects without invoking anything with combined properties of abstractness and agency.

definitions.plain_definition: Relating to the study of knowledge — how we know what we know.
definitions.used_in_context: epistemological

definitions.plain_definition: Relating to the study of existence and reality — what kinds of things exist.
definitions.used_in_context: ontological priority

definitions.plain_definition: A Greek word meaning 'word,' 'reason,' or 'principle.' In theology, it refers to the divine reason or order that structures the universe.
definitions.used_in_context: I believe the universe is structured by something that looks exactly like what theologians call the Logos.

definitions.plain_definition: A made-up term in this document meaning a rule that requires you to state your own starting beliefs before criticizing someone else's.
definitions.used_in_context: The Biaxiosum Rule

definitions.plain_definition: A physical law that says the strength of a force (like gravity or light) gets weaker by the square of the distance from its source.
definitions.used_in_context: The inverse-square law governed gravitational attraction before any mind formalized it.

definitions.plain_definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system. The second law of thermodynamics says entropy always increases in a closed system.
definitions.used_in_context: Thermodynamic systems obeyed the laws of entropy.

definitions.plain_definition: The second law of thermodynamics: in a closed system, entropy (disorder) always increases over time.
definitions.used_in_context: No closed system can reverse its own entropy

definitions.plain_definition: Refers to Landauer's principle: any information processing has a minimum energy cost, related to heat and entropy.
definitions.used_in_context: Information processing has irreducible thermodynamic cost

definitions.plain_definition: Refers to Gödel's incompleteness theorems: in any consistent mathematical system, there are true statements that cannot be proven within that system.
definitions.used_in_context: No consistent formal system can prove its own consistency

definitions.plain_definition: Refers to Tarski's undefinability theorem: no formal language can define its own truth predicate (what 'true' means within that language).
definitions.used_in_context: No formal language can define its own truth predicate

definitions.plain_definition: Refers to the halting problem: no algorithm can determine whether an arbitrary computer program will eventually stop or run forever.
definitions.used_in_context: No algorithm can determine whether an arbitrary program halts

definitions.plain_definition: A type of geometry that does not follow Euclid's rules, especially the rule that parallel lines never meet. Used to describe curved space in Einstein's theory of relativity.
definitions.used_in_context: Non-Euclidean geometry was developed as a mathematical curiosity in the 19th century. Einstein used it to describe spacetime curvature in 1915.

definitions.plain_definition: Numbers that have both a real part and an imaginary part (involving the square root of -1). They are essential in quantum mechanics.
definitions.used_in_context: Complex numbers were invented as algebraic abstractions. Quantum mechanics requires them as fundamental.

definitions.plain_definition: A branch of mathematics that studies symmetry and the ways objects can be combined and transformed.
definitions.used_in_context: Group theory was developed as pure mathematics. Particle physics is built on it.

definitions.plain_definition: A fundamental equation in quantum mechanics that describes how the quantum state of a physical system changes over time.
definitions.used_in_context: Quantum mechanical processes followed the Schrödinger equation.

definitions.plain_definition: A set of four equations that describe how electricity and magnetism work and how they are related.
definitions.used_in_context: Electromagnetic radiation obeyed Maxwell's equations.

definitions.plain_definition: An argument that avoids the real issue by playing with the meaning of words instead of addressing the facts.
definitions.used_in_context: This is a semantic dodge.

definitions.plain_definition: Applying something from the present back to an earlier time, as if it were true then too.
definitions.used_in_context: how a human invention retroactively governed the behavior of a universe that predated its inventors

definitions.plain_definition: Existed before something else.
definitions.used_in_context: a universe that predated its inventors by 13.8 billion years

definitions.plain_definition: Two different ways of looking at or representing the same underlying reality.
definitions.used_in_context: I believe mathematical truth and divine truth are dual projections of the same invariant structure.

definitions.plain_definition: A pattern or set of relationships that stays the same even when other things change.
definitions.used_in_context: I believe mathematical truth and divine truth are dual projections of the same invariant structure.

definitions.plain_definition: A statement that has been proven to be true using logic and reasoning.
definitions.used_in_context: Five independent results from five independent fields converge on the same structural conclusion

definitions.plain_definition: A set of symbols and rules for manipulating them, used to do mathematics or logic in a precise way.
definitions.used_in_context: No consistent formal system can prove its own consistency

definitions.plain_definition: A way of saying 'this statement is true' within a formal language.
definitions.used_in_context: No formal language can define its own truth predicate

definitions.plain_definition: The minimum amount of energy that must be used (and turned into heat) to perform a task, like processing information.
definitions.used_in_context: Information processing has irreducible thermodynamic cost

definitions.plain_definition: Cannot be made smaller or simpler. The minimum possible.
definitions.used_in_context: Information processing has irreducible thermodynamic cost

definitions.plain_definition: A system that does not exchange matter or energy with its surroundings.
definitions.used_in_context: No closed system can reverse its own entropy

definitions.plain_definition: Admitting that part of an opposing argument is true.
definitions.used_in_context: But that concession is fatal.

definitions.plain_definition: Here, it means the concession destroys the argument completely.
definitions.used_in_context: But that concession is fatal.

definitions.plain_definition: A situation where you have to choose between two bad options.
definitions.used_in_context: The Platonist faces a dilemma.

definitions.plain_definition: Says the opposite of something else. Cannot both be true.
definitions.used_in_context: which contradicts their abstractness

definitions.plain_definition: The quality of being an idea or concept, not a physical thing.
definitions.used_in_context: which contradicts their abstractness
